title: The recorded century
subtitle: Performers on record: acoustic horn and microphone

hero.caption: Francis Barraud, His Master’s Voice, 1898–99. Nipper the dog listens at the horn of a gramophone.

intro: In Milan in 1902, Caruso and a pianist recorded Vesti la giubba into a recording horn. In the 1920s, microphones recorded Rachmaninoff’s piano playing and Chaliapin’s bass voice, and the records preserved every slowing and quickening of their phrasing.

stations.title: Caruso and Cottone, Milan
stations.text: On 30 November 1902 in Milan, Enrico Caruso recorded Vesti la giubba with Salvatore Cottone at the piano. Both performed into a horn. Sound entering the horn vibrated a diaphragm, which moved the stylus cutting the groove, so the voices and instruments supplied all the energy themselves. In acoustic studios, a performer’s distance from the horn could determine whether an accompaniment was audible or overwhelmed the singer. On this recording Cottone’s piano plays separate, percussive notes beneath Caruso’s sustained tenor. In the aria, Leoncavallo’s clown Canio has to perform despite his grief.

cues.text: Cottone accompanies Caruso at the piano.
The tenor’s phrase grows again above the piano’s separate attacks.
Caruso sustains the broad phrase while Cottone keeps the accompaniment moving.
Voice and piano close the short side.

stations.title: The clown with orchestral accompaniment
stations.text: Here an orchestra accompanies Caruso. On this Victor side the instruments can sustain a phrase beneath his voice, where Cottone’s piano had to strike each note and let it decay. Canio begins with the outburst of the recitative, then orders himself into his costume. In Leoncavallo’s Pagliacci, the audience has paid and expects to laugh, and the performer must turn his own tears into the clown’s grimaces. Caruso sings the command on long vowels. The orchestra plays beneath him as the melody broadens.

cues.text: Caruso begins Canio’s recitative, now with orchestral accompaniment.
The voice eases before the next expansion of the phrase.
Sustained notes in the orchestra accompany the tenor’s melody.
Canio’s command to laugh, set as a long lament.

stations.title: Beethoven and the side limit
stations.text: On 10 November 1913, Nikisch and the Berlin Philharmonic recorded Beethoven’s Fifth. Recording an orchestra acoustically called for special measures. Stroh string instruments, fitted with aluminium horns, reinforced the ordinary strings and directed their sound towards the recording horn. Nikisch also had to fit the music on the disc. At his broad tempo, the exposition repeat of the first movement would have overrun the first side, so he left it out, and the exposition is heard only once.

cues.text: Nikisch and the Berlin Philharmonic recorded the complete symphony in a single day.
The exposition is played without its written repeat.

stations.title: Paderewski and rubato
stations.text: Paderewski recorded Chopin’s F♯ major Nocturne in New York on 14 May 1917. His hands often play separately: the accompaniment sounds first and the melody follows it. Chords can be spread from bottom to top. In his essay for Henry T. Finck’s Success in Music and How It Is Won (1909), Paderewski rejected, for soloists, the rule that time borrowed in one phrase must be paid back in another: “What is lost is lost.” Chopin’s doppio movimento doubles the pace for the middle section.

cues.text: The melody rests on its accompaniment, which leaves room for Paderewski to sound his hands separately.
The upper line plays the melody freely over the piano’s supporting notes.
Chopin’s doppio movimento makes the middle section quicker.
The loud middle section gets quieter before the opening song returns.

stations.title: Rachmaninoff’s Edison recordings

art.caption: Konstantin Somov, Sergei Rachmaninoff, 1925, six years after the pianist’s Edison session.

stations.text: Rachmaninoff recorded the Prelude for Edison in 1919; it was a piece he had brought with him from Russia. The Diamond Disc was issued to buyers in December 1920. The excerpt begins at the Agitato, where triplets carry the tune towards the return of the opening chords. The score sets that return out on four staves, although only two hands are playing. The chords then die away into the quiet coda, and the last sounds are widely spaced.

cues.text: The melody runs through triplets towards the chordal return.
The opening call returns, written on four staves for the pianist’s two hands.
Quiet, widely spaced chords finish the coda.

stations.title: Prelude: second sitting
stations.text: Two years later, Rachmaninoff recorded the Prelude again, for Victor. The studio still recorded through a horn. The quick central passage follows the quiet opening and drives towards the familiar chords, here recorded on another day by another company. He presses the triplets forwards and still gives the returning chords ample room. In this performance the chordal return is already close when the excerpt begins. After it, in the coda, the hands move apart and the dynamic falls to quiet.

cues.text: After the quiet opening, the piano moves in the agitated middle section.
The broad chords return across the keyboard.
The piano moves from the large chords to a quiet close.

stations.title: The microphone
stations.text: By the time Rachmaninoff returned to the Prelude in New York on 4 April 1928, Victor had changed its machinery. A microphone turned the piano’s sound into an electrical signal, and amplification supplied the energy to drive the cutting stylus. Victor and Columbia had introduced the process commercially in 1925; it captured a wider range of sound. The issued performance was take 23. Rachmaninoff had written the piece, with its triplets and heavy chords, thirty-six years earlier. It ends with a quiet coda.

cues.text: The triplets lead into the return of the chords.
The opening call sounds in the broad chordal passage.
The coda drops from the loud dynamic of the return and ends on soft chords.

stations.title: Chaliapin’s acoustic recording of The Prophet, 1921
stations.text: On 10 October 1921, at Hayes, Chaliapin recorded Rimsky-Korsakov’s The Prophet, with Percy Pitt conducting the orchestra. Pushkin’s poem of 1826 begins with a thirsty wanderer in a dark desert. A six-winged angel opens his eyes and ears, tears out his tongue and replaces his heart with a burning coal. The bass narrates these events before delivering God’s command. The opening is measured and close to speech. At the end the score is marked con forza e maestoso, forcefully and majestically.

cues.text: Chaliapin’s measured bass phrases open Pushkin’s vision.
The voice continues above a flowing accompaniment.
A quiet orchestral passage connects the sung phrases.
The opening tempo returns.
The bass sings the final command, marked con forza e maestoso.

stations.title: The Prophet: the electrical recording, 1927
stations.text: On 20 October 1927 Chaliapin recorded The Prophet in London with Albert Coates, six years after the acoustic side with Percy Pitt. In this electrical recording he sings Pushkin’s text again and takes more time over the whole song. There are quiet orchestral passages between the main vocal declamations. In the last section God commands the remade man to cross seas and lands and set human hearts alight with his words. Chaliapin sings this command above a busy accompaniment. After his last syllable the orchestra continues to the final chords.

cues.text: Chaliapin shapes the opening in measured, speech-like phrases.
The accompaniment moves beneath the sustained bass line.
A quiet orchestral passage leaves space between the vocal phrases.
The opening pace returns before the final command.
The bass sings above the running accompaniment.
The accompaniment continues after the last sung phrase to the closing chords.
